# The Causal Boundary: Matter, Momentum, and the Co-Design Challenge

![Systems Organ Focus: Tracing the Causal Boundary across the complete agent pipeline. Chapter 1 establishes the foundational loop coupling the sensory-motor lifecycle to irreversible physical state transitions across the Proposal and Permission Privilege Boundary.](figures/fig_pipeline_locator.svg){#fig-locator-ch01 width=100%}

This chapter draws the line that separates ordinary machine learning from Physical AI: when a learned computation stops being advisory software and starts permanently changing matter and energy, and why that crossing is not another remote procedure call. You will meet the proposal–permission split that keeps stochastic models from holding motor authority, the co-design matrix that organizes the rest of the book, and the loop charter that records what must already be true before later chapters request motion. Perception, planning, and enforcement only make sense after that boundary and privilege split are clear.

::: {.callout-objective}
By the conclusion of this chapter, you will be able to:

1. Formulate the causal feedback boundary that contrasts digital open-loop computation with closed-loop physical irreversibility ($A_t \to W_{t+1} \to O_{t+1}$), and explain why software cannot undo kinetic energy or thermal dissipation.
2. Bound physical limits with SI reasoning across kinetic momentum ($\mathbf{p} = m\mathbf{v}$), winding Joule heating ($I^2 R$), inductive rise time, and mechanical non-idealities, including at least one worked numerical example.
3. Architect a proposal–permission privilege split that keeps untrusted neural policies on Linux application processors away from deterministic bare-metal safety supervisors on microcontrollers.
4. State the two axes of the Physical AI co-design matrix and read each cell as a systems question reserved for later chapters.
5. Trace the three-part curriculum progression from foundations through the embodied sensory-motor lifecycle to heterogeneous placement and defensible release.
:::

## Crossing the Threshold

Connect a policy script to the gate drivers of an electric motor inverter, the steering rack of a delivery rover, or the proportional valve of a hydraulic actuator, and the variables in your code cease to be abstract bits in RAM. A floating-point number is transduced into pulse-width modulated switching sequences in hardware timer registers. Those gate signals switch three-phase MOSFET bridges across a DC bus, driving amperes of phase current through copper stator windings to generate magnetic flux that accelerates kilograms of aluminum, steel, and glass through three-dimensional space.

The instant computation moves matter, digital undo disappears:

$$\begin{aligned}
\text{Digital World: } &\text{Software Exception} \xrightarrow{\quad \text{try/catch} \quad} \text{HTTP 500 Retry} \quad (W_t \text{ Unchanged}) \\
\text{Physical AI: } &\text{Actuation } A_t \implies \text{Matter Mutates } (W_t \longrightarrow W_{t+1}) \implies O_{t+1}
\end{aligned}$$

Kinetic momentum ($\mathbf{p} = m\mathbf{v}$) cannot be erased by software.^[For an articulated $n$-link manipulator, the total kinetic energy is $E_k = \frac{1}{2}\dot{\mathbf{q}}^T \mathbf{M}(\mathbf{q})\dot{\mathbf{q}}$, where $\mathbf{M}(\mathbf{q})$ is the configuration-dependent generalized inertia tensor. Even if motor drive commands drop to zero, velocity decays only through physical friction, counter-torques, or impact.] Excessive continuous current accumulates irreversible Joule heat ($I^2 R$) that degrades insulation and demagnetizes magnets.^[The thermal rise in motor windings follows $\Delta T(t) = \int_{0}^{t} \frac{I^2(\tau) R - \Delta T(\tau) / R_{\text{th}}}{C_{\text{th}}} \, d\tau$, where $R_{\text{th}}$ and $C_{\text{th}}$ are the thermal resistance and capacitance of the stator assembly.] The footnotes name the governing physics; a worked numerical bound appears later in this chapter under silicon and steel, and Chapter 2 turns freshness and stopping into ledger numbers.

Nor does a software crash restore a safe electrical state. When an application processor dies, the operating system may reclaim virtual memory while hardware timer peripherals on an independent clock tree keep pulsing gate drivers at the last written duty cycle. Software crashes do not de-energize copper coils.

## The Causal Feedback Loop and Irreversibility

A Physical AI system differs from digital machine learning, classical automation, and simple embedded sensing in one structural way: learned software may permanently change the world, and the next observation is already conditioned on that change.

::: {.callout-definition title="Physical AI Systems"}
**Physical AI Systems** is the systems engineering discipline for machines where learned foundation models exercise delegated physical authority across the analog and digital boundary under irreversible physical laws and hard real-time constraints.

Unlike digital machine learning systems, every permitted physical action irreversibly mutates the state of the physical world ($W_t \to W_{t+1}$) and endogenously alters all future sensory observations ($A_t \to W_{t+1} \to O_{t+1}$).
:::

### An Autopsy That Recurs

The same failure returns throughout this book in different costumes. Here is its clearest form.

::: {.callout-autopsy title="Latched Duty Cycle After Host Crash"}
* **System:** Six-degree-of-freedom tabletop manipulator running a vision-language-action policy with direct host write access to motor timer registers.
* **Incident:** The arm crushed an aluminum calibration fixture at $1.2\text{ m/s}$ and sheared the wrist cycloidal drive pins.
* **Telemetry Snapshot:** At $T+12.410\text{ s}$ the Linux application processor emitted a motor current target. Two milliseconds later an unhandled lighting reflection produced a zero-detection exception in an open-vocabulary detector, and the Python runtime crashed. Capture and compare registers remained latched at $78\%$ duty cycle on an independent silicon clock tree.
* **Root Cause:** When the operating system reclaimed the process’s virtual memory, memory-mapped timer peripherals kept pulsing gate drivers. The inverter continued driving phase current into the stator windings until impact.
* **Architectural Flaw:** Monolithic authority—learned software held direct electrical control over motor timers with no independent real-time permission supervisor on dedicated microcontroller silicon.
* **Provenance:** Engineered composite. The mechanism and failure path are drawn from documented incident classes; the system, telemetry, and costs are constructed for teaching and are not a report of a specific event.
:::

The arm did not fail because the model was “not accurate enough.” It failed because a stochastic proposal path held direct electrical authority, and a crash on the application processor did not revoke that authority. That single architectural flaw motivates the privilege split later in this chapter and the enforcement work that follows.

### The Three Universal Defining Properties

Across embodiments—from humanoids to energy infrastructure—three properties jointly mark a **Physical AI System**.

First, the system includes a **learned foundation component**. It does not rely exclusively on hardcoded if-then rules or pre-programmed CAD trajectories. Vision-language-action models, latent world models, and diffusion policies generalize over unstructured, open-world environments.

Second, it **operates across the analog and digital boundary**. Discrete clock ticks, token embeddings, and tensor matrices directly command continuous analog energy fluxes: three-phase inverters, PWM gate drivers, hydraulic valves, magnetic flux, chemical reaction rates.

Third, it is **governed by irreversible physical laws**. Every permitted action permanently mutates matter and energy ($W_t \to W_{t+1}$). If an algorithm hallucinates or a latency tail spikes, the risk is not a bad log line—it is collision, sheared gear teeth, thermal runaway ($I^2R$), or injury.

### The Four Bedrock Laws

Every architectural interface, firmware driver, and release checkpoint in this book is anchored in four laws. The callouts state them for reference; the bridges show how each appears on a machine.

::: {.callout-law title="1. Physical Causality and Irreversibility"}
Software state can be caught with an exception block, isolated in a container, or rolled back. Physical actions ($W_t \to W_{t+1}$) governed by mass, inertia, friction ($\mu$), and gravity ($g$) are permanent and irreversible. Every actuation permanently alters the physical environment, dissipates energy, and alters all future sensory observations endogenously ($A_t \to W_{t+1} \to O_{t+1}$).
:::

That is why a crashed Python process is not a contained incident once PWM registers remain latched: the world has already moved, and the next observation is conditioned on that move.

::: {.callout-law title="2. Information Freshness (The Time Law)"}
The physical world does not pause while an AI model computes. Sensor observations age the microsecond photons strike the photodiode. Mean latency ($P_{50}$) is a dangerous illusion; tail latency ($P_{99}$), memory bus contention, and information age ($\Delta t$) dictate physical closed-loop stability and dynamic stopping distances ($d_{\text{stop}}$).
:::

Chapter 2 develops this law quantitatively—waterfall budgets, freshness walls, and stopping envelopes. Here it is enough to notice that “average FPS” never appears in a stopping-distance inequality—tails do.

::: {.callout-law title="3. Proposal and Permission Privilege (The Architecture Law)"}
No stochastic, learned neural network (VLM, VLA, or Diffusion Policy) may hold direct motor authority. Learned models running on application processors are *untrusted proposal services*. Real-time physical permission belongs exclusively to dedicated, zero-allocation microcontrollers running deterministic mathematical safety envelopes and physical fallbacks.
:::

The autopsy above is this law in negative form: when proposal and permission share one privilege domain, a model failure becomes a mechanical failure.

::: {.callout-law title="4. Governed Change and Defensible Release (The Safety Law)"}
A physical agent shapes its own future data distribution. Naive training on raw operational logs without isolating safety interventions induces severe covariate shift and policy collapse. A cherry-picked video demo or simulation benchmark is not evidence of safety; defensible release requires cross-layer fault injection and a formal safety case rendering an accountable release verdict.
:::

Parts II and III return to this law when overrides, logging, and Claim-Argument-Evidence release verdicts become first-class artifacts (Chapters 10–11). The law is stated here so later chapters inherit a shared obligation; the protocols are not taught yet.


## Archetypes, Agents, and the Embodiment Spectrum

The three properties and four laws apply to every embodiment. A textbook still needs recurring machines on which to hang the mathematics, so we distill three interaction archetypes (@tbl-canonical-archetypes), contrast digital agents with physical agents (@tbl-digital-vs-physical), and then widen the lens across domains (@tbl-embodiment-spectrum).

### Three Canonical Archetypes

**Mobility** covers systems that move their own mass through free space—rovers, humanoids, drones, vehicles. The governing physics is momentum ($\mathbf{p} = m\mathbf{v}$); the governing systems question is whether stopping distance still fits inside remaining clearance when latency tails stretch.

**Contact manipulation** covers systems that touch, grasp, cut, or deform external matter in $SE(3)$. Contact stiffness, friction ($\mu$), and torque rates ($\dot{\boldsymbol{\tau}}$) dominate, and step-wise neural waypoints that look smooth on a plot can still shear gear teeth. This is our primary teaching spine.

**Energy and process** covers systems that regulate continuous analog state without spatial travel—battery thermal loops, grid inverters, closed-loop medical devices. Whenever a learned model may change irreversible physical state, the same causal boundary applies, whether or not the machine looks like a robot.

| Dimension | Archetype 1: Mobility | Archetype 2: Contact Manipulation | Archetype 3: Energy and Process |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Interaction** | Moving in free space | Touching and shaping matter | Regulating state flows |
| **Physical Law** | Momentum ($\mathbf{p} = m\mathbf{v}$), stopping bounds | Contact forces, torque rate ($\dot{\boldsymbol{\tau}}$) | Thermodynamics ($I^2R$), conservation |
| **Silicon Tension** | Sensory DMA and $P_{99}$ latency tails | Multi-rate IPC and continuous jerk | Sampling lag and thermal safe sets |
| **Examples** | Humanoids, rovers, vehicles, drones | Manipulators, grippers, surgical tools | Battery thermal loops, grid inverters, infusion pumps |
| **Pedagogical Role** | Time, latency, stopping distance | Primary teaching spine | Scope beyond robotics |

: The Three Canonical Archetypes of Physical AI. {#tbl-canonical-archetypes}

### Digital Agents versus Physical Agents

The word *agent* is overloaded. Software engineers build digital agents—large language models wired to scrapers, code interpreters, databases, and chat interfaces. Those systems can reason and tool-call, but they live in forgiving virtual environments. Failure raises an exception, a container restarts, a transaction rolls back, a client retries. Nothing irreversible happened to matter.

A physical agent is a different engineering object (@tbl-digital-vs-physical). Its outputs are not JSON payloads: they switch PWM gate drivers, accelerate mechanical mass, draw current across inductive coils, and permanently alter the environment.

| Dimension | The Digital Agent | The Physical Agent |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Operational Realm** | Virtual sandboxes, APIs, browsers, databases | Physical matter, 3D space, kinetic energy ($W_t \to W_{t+1}$) |
| **Execution Medium** | Python runtimes, cloud VMs, serverless containers | Heterogeneous silicon: Linux MPU + bare-metal real-time MCU |
| **Error Handling** | Exception handlers, HTTP retries, transactional rollbacks | Collisions, Joule heating ($I^2R$), gearbox damage |
| **Time Model** | Turn-based, asynchronous, unbounded wait states | Continuous real-time, microsecond freshness ($\Delta t$), $P_{99}$ tails |
| **Action Authority** | Emits JSON, tool calls, or text tokens | Emits PWM switching, motor torques, and physical force |
| **Safety Paradigm** | Guardrails, prompt filters, schema validation | Control barrier invariants, stopping bounds ($d_{\text{stop}}$), hardware interlocks |

: Digital Agents versus Physical Agents. {#tbl-digital-vs-physical}

### Success Is Dual

In digital machine learning, performance is evaluated along a statistical dimension: average test accuracy or loss over a dataset. In classical automation, performance is evaluated along a deterministic dimension: invariant satisfaction within a structured workcell.

In **Physical AI Systems**, success is dual and non-negotiable:

$$\text{Physical AI Success} = \underbrace{\text{Semantic Competence}}_{\text{Task achieved from sensor input}} \quad \mathbf{AND} \quad \underbrace{\text{Physical Invariant Survival}}_{\text{Zero collisions or hardware damage}}$$

A vision-language-action model that successfully grasps a target object 99 times out of 100, but shears a cycloidal gearbox or strikes an obstacle on the 100th attempt, is a failed system. Physical AI systems engineering maximizes semantic competence while mathematically guaranteeing that catastrophic invariant violations cannot occur.

### The Causal Boundary Test

To decide whether an engineering system sits inside Physical AI, apply a three-part test (@tbl-causal-boundary): learned model, analog–digital authority, and irreversible physical consequence.

| System Type | Learned Model? | Analog–Digital Boundary? | Irreversible ($W_{t+1}$)? | Classification |
| :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :--- |
| **Industrial PLC** | No (PID / state logic) | Yes | Yes | Classical automation |
| **Diagnostic radiology AI** | Yes | No (screen only) | No | Advisory digital software |
| **Teleoperated surgical robot** | Yes (filtering) | Yes | Yes | Shared-control teleoperation |
| **Autonomous robotic arm** | Yes (VLA / diffusion) | Yes | Yes | **Physical AI (Archetype 2)** |
| **Autonomous vehicle / drone** | Yes (trajectory planner) | Yes | Yes | **Physical AI (Archetype 1)** |
| **Smart grid inverter** | Yes (load predictor) | Yes | Yes | **Physical AI (Archetype 3)** |

: The Causal Boundary Classification. {#tbl-causal-boundary}

If an algorithm draws bounding boxes for a human to inspect, it is advisory. The instant software directly commands a motorized actuator or energizes an interlock without human confirmation, it crosses the Causal Boundary.

### The Embodiment Spectrum

Benchtop manipulators make excellent teaching platforms, but **Physical AI is not a robotics-only discipline**. It is the systems craft for *any* machine where learned software exercises delegated authority over matter and energy (@tbl-embodiment-spectrum). Across domains, the same contract applies: high-capacity models on application processors act as **untrusted proposal services**; deterministic real-time supervisors hold **permission authority** over inverters, relays, valves, and clamps.

| Embodiment Domain | Untrusted Proposal Engine (MPU) | Physical Matter & Energy ($W_t \to W_{t+1}$) | Trusted Permission Authority (MCU) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Mobility & Aerospace** | Neural trajectory planner | Kinetic momentum, steering angle, friction ($\mu$) | Brake-by-wire and steering envelope supervisor |
| **Grid & High-Voltage** | Learned battery dispatch predictor | Mega-joule current flow, inverter heating | Microsecond over-current and thermal relay |
| **Active Medical Devices** | Neural glucose and drug-rate predictor | Insulin volume, biochemical concentration | Hard-limited stepper clamp and dose watchdog |
| **Precision Manufacturing** | Vision toolpath and laser router | Spindle torque, laser thermal fluence | Axis limit enforcer and optical E-stop |
| **Autonomous Robotics** | VLA diffusion action-chunk decoder | Joint torque, linkage inertia, contact force | $1\text{ kHz}$ bare-metal Control Barrier Function |

: The Physical AI Embodiment Spectrum. {#tbl-embodiment-spectrum}

Read the spectrum left to right: what proposes, what physical quantity changes, and what silicon is allowed to refuse. The reference kit used with this book maps to the robotics row; the same privilege split is what a grid inverter or infusion pump needs when a learned predictor is in the loop.

### Policy Endogeneity and Compounding Error

In digital machine learning, datasets are often treated as independent and identically distributed ($i.i.d.$). In Physical AI, the system is locked in an endogenous causal loop:

$$A_t \longrightarrow W_{t+1} \longrightarrow O_{t+1}$$

Every action $A_t$ mutates the world into $W_{t+1}$, which generates the next observation $O_{t+1}$. In standard supervised learning, test error scales roughly linearly with horizon $\mathcal{O}(T \epsilon)$. In sequential physical systems, a small steering mistake pushes the machine outside its training distribution; the policy then errs more severely, and divergence can grow quadratically with horizon $\mathcal{O}(T^2 \epsilon)$ [@ross2011reduction].

Safety overrides intensify the problem. When a supervisor rejects a dangerous proposal, it alters the physical trajectory. If telemetry logs those transitions without tagging them as interventions, retraining on raw logs teaches the model that dangerous paths were nominal. Slicing and tagging interventions is a central governance requirement examined in Chapter 10.


## Physical Constraints in Silicon and Steel

When software leaves the datacenter sandbox and interacts with physical matter, four realities assert themselves (@tbl-software-vs-physics). Simulation often hides them: actions become instantaneous state assignments, torques appear without inductive lag, and collisions yield scalar penalties without plastic deformation. On the bench, electrical energy becomes kinetic momentum through nonlinear magnetic fields; windings accumulate Joule heat; gearboxes show backlash and wear; DMA buffers contend for shared memory bandwidth; and collisions shear drive pins.

### Kinetic Momentum and Mechanical Inertia ($\mathbf{p} = m\mathbf{v}$)

In digital software, a running loop can be paused with a breakpoint. In the physical realm, mass $m$ moving at velocity $\mathbf{v}$ carries kinetic momentum $\mathbf{p} = m\mathbf{v}$ and kinetic energy

$$E_k = \frac{1}{2} m \|\mathbf{v}\|^2 \quad \text{or, for articulated linkages, } E_k = \frac{1}{2} \dot{\mathbf{q}}^T \mathbf{M}(\mathbf{q}) \dot{\mathbf{q}},$$

where $\mathbf{M}(\mathbf{q})$ is the configuration-dependent generalized inertia tensor. If an application processor freezes, momentum continues to carry the mechanism forward. The mass stops only when counter-torques, friction, or impact remove the energy. Software cannot instantly zero kinetic energy.

A kit-scale thought calculation makes the point without waiting for Chapter 2’s full stopping ledger. Take the autopsy regime: end-effector speed $v = 1.2\text{ m/s}$. If timer registers remain latched for only $\Delta t = 50\text{ ms}$ after the host dies, the mechanism still travels

$$d_{\text{coast}} = v \cdot \Delta t = (1.2\text{ m/s})(0.050\text{ s}) = 0.060\text{ m} = 60\text{ mm}$$

before any new deceleration command can even be written. Sixty millimeters is enough to crush a calibration fixture or shear a wrist pin; the number did not require a neural network, only velocity and a permission outage. Kinetic energy at that speed for a $0.40\text{ kg}$ tooling mass is $E_k = \frac{1}{2} m v^2 = 0.288\text{ J}$—small by industrial standards, still irreversible once it enters the fixture. Chapter 2 will fold the same arithmetic into $d_{\text{stop}}(v, \Delta t)$ under measured $P_{99}$ tails; here the lesson is that latched authority has a distance cost you can compute on the back of a notebook page.

### Joule Heating and Thermal Accumulation ($I^2 R$)

Driving motor current $I(t)$ across stator winding resistance $R$ produces continuous thermal dissipation:

$$Q(t) = \int_{0}^{t} I^2(\tau) R \, d\tau.$$

Copper and iron tolerate brief acceleration bursts by absorbing heat into thermal capacitance $C_{\text{th}}$, but steady-state current must remain below the continuous rating $I_{\text{cont}}$. A bug or stall that commands continuous stall current for even a few seconds can exceed insulation limits, damage enamel, and demagnetize rotor magnets. Deriving $I_{\text{cont}}$ from $R$, $R_{\text{th}}$, and a temperature rise budget is Chapter 2’s thermal column; this chapter only requires that heat be treated as a hard bound, not a peak-torque marketing number.

### Electromagnetic Actuation and Inductive Rise Time

In idealized simulation, commanded torque $\tau_t$ appears instantly. In copper and silicon, phase current cannot jump discontinuously because of stator inductance $L$:

$$V(t) = R I(t) + L \frac{dI(t)}{dt} + K_e \omega(t),$$

where $K_e \omega(t)$ is back-electromotive force. The electrical time constant $\tau_e = L / R$ inserts rise time before magnetic flux builds; back-EMF further limits torque at high speed and enforces a voltage saturation boundary.

### Mechanical Non-Idealities: Backlash, Compliance, and Jerk

Real transmissions are not rigid mathematical linkages. Cycloidal and harmonic drives exhibit gear-tooth backlash—angular deadbands where motor rotation produces no output torque until contact is re-established. Discontinuous torque commands ($\dot{\boldsymbol{\tau}} \to \infty$, or jerk $\dddot{\mathbf{q}}$) create shock that chips teeth and shears pins. On contact, impact force scales with stiffness ($F = k \Delta x$); without sub-millisecond reflexes, rigid impacts exceed structural ratings.

| Physical Phenomenon | Software Assumption (Sim) | Bench Reality | Systems Impact |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Momentum ($\mathbf{p} = m\mathbf{v}$)** | Velocity drops to $0$ instantly | Finite stopping distance $d_{\text{stop}}$ | Collision if latency delays braking |
| **Joule Heating ($I^2 R$)** | Unlimited peak torque | Overheats under sustained current | Stall current damages stator coils |
| **Inductance ($\tau_e = L/R$)** | Torque responds in $0\text{ ms}$ | Current rises exponentially | Phase lag degrades stability |
| **Backlash** | Continuous kinematic chain | Deadband during reversals | Oscillation on direction changes |
| **Jerk ($\dddot{\mathbf{q}}$)** | Step acceleration allowed | Mechanical shock | Sheared pins and tooth fatigue |

: Digital software assumptions versus physical hardware realities. {#tbl-software-vs-physics}


## The Proposal and Permission Privilege Split

A common misconception in modern deep learning is the monolithic fallacy: that scaling a single end-to-end network—from raw pixels to raw motor PWM—will eliminate classical control, real-time operating systems, and hardware safety supervisors.

That model violates fault containment, privilege separation, and real-time determinism [@saltzer1984end; @brooks1986robust]. Neural networks are statistical approximators; under rare lighting, occlusion, or out-of-distribution scenes they will eventually emit an erratic action vector. Wiring those weights straight to motor timers guarantees eventual hardware destruction. Application operating systems prioritize throughput over latency determinism: page faults, garbage collection, and preemption produce multi-millisecond tails ($P_{99} > 100\text{ ms}$) that a $1000\text{ Hz}$ motor loop cannot absorb. And if a user-space process crashes—as in the autopsy above—the motor power stage must still be governed by an independent processor that remains alive.

![The Anatomy and Causal Sensory-Motor Loop of a Physical AI Agent. Tracing the canonical pipeline organs across the Proposal and Permission Privilege Boundary separating untrusted Linux MPU proposals from trusted bare-metal MCU enforcement.](figures/fig01_agent_anatomy.svg){#fig-anatomy width=100%}

### The Two-Brain Architecture

We split the substrate into two execution tiers across a hardware bus firewall (@fig-anatomy).

The **untrusted proposal engine**—a Linux MPU or NPU—runs high-capacity learned models: multimodal vision-language reasoning at roughly $0.5\text{--}2\text{ Hz}$ and diffusion action-chunk policies at $20\text{--}50\text{ Hz}$. It lives in rich virtual memory with dynamic allocation, emits time-bounded candidate proposals ($p_t$) into a shared SRAM mailbox, and holds **zero** direct electrical authority over motor gate drivers.

The **trusted permission authority**—a bare-metal MCU—runs a deterministic $1000\text{ Hz}$ safety supervisor and high-frequency current loops in zero-wait-state static SRAM with no dynamic heap. It evaluates mathematical safety envelopes and dynamic stopping inequalities ($d_{\text{stop}} \le d_{\text{clearance}}$), projecting candidate proposals onto a forward-invariant safe set. The detailed Control Barrier Function quadratic program

$$u_t = \arg\min_{u \in \mathcal{U}_{\text{safe}}} \|u - p_t\|^2 \quad \text{subject to } h(\mathbf{x}) \ge 0$$

and field-oriented current loops are owned by Chapter 8 [@ames2019control]; what this chapter requires is only the privilege claim: the MCU alone may write PWM timer registers and gate-enable lines, and it may refuse or reshape any MPU proposal.

On a timeout, refusal is not optional philosophy. Treat the proposal path as holding an expiring lease with a heartbeat. If the shared mailbox age or heartbeat gap exceeds a hard budget—$\tau_{\text{heartbeat}} = 20\text{ ms}$ on the reference kit—the MCU discards the candidate, freezes or decelerates under its own law, and escalates toward Safe Torque Off. That single timing rule is how “the model crashed” becomes “the motors still stopped.” Chapter 6 deepens lease fields and abstention; here the mechanism is only age $\to$ revoke.

The Arduino UNO Q reference kit makes the split observable on the bench. The Linux application processor (Qualcomm Dragonwing) runs proposal software and may publish candidates into a shared mailbox; the STM32 microcontroller alone is wired for real-time timer and gate-enable authority. A student can therefore prove privilege without trusting a vendor slogan: kill or stall the host proposal process and confirm that PWM does not remain an MPU-owned open loop.

::: {.callout-contract}
| Component | Substrate | Contract Specification |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| MPU proposes | Untrusted · Linux MPU | Candidate action chunk $\mathbf{a}_{t:t+H}$; expiring intent lease with issue time and TTL; heartbeat period $\le 20\text{ ms}$; zero direct electrical authority over motor gate drivers |
| MCU permits | Trusted · bare-metal MCU | Validates joint limits, velocity bounds, and stopping clearance; projects or rejects proposals under safe-set constraints (CBF detail in Ch 8); sole privilege to write PWM registers and toggle gate enable |
| Failure escalation | MCU hardware reflex | On lease expiration, heartbeat stall ($> 20\text{ ms}$), or invariant breach, revoke PWM and execute controlled dynamic braking toward Safe Torque Off |
:::

| Dimension | Untrusted Proposal Engine (MPU / Linux) | Trusted Permission Authority (MCU) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Compute** | Multi-core ARM Cortex-A + neural accelerator | Single-core ARM Cortex-M / RISC-V |
| **OS** | Linux (best-effort / Preempt-RT) | Bare-metal / FreeRTOS (deterministic) |
| **Memory** | Multi-gigabyte DRAM (shared bus) | Static SRAM / TCM (zero heap) |
| **Workloads** | Vision transformers, world models, diffusion ACT | Barrier invariants, watchdogs, current loops (FOC detail in Ch 8) |
| **Timing Horizon** | $20\text{ ms}$ to $2000\text{ ms}$ ($0.5\text{--}50\text{ Hz}$) | $1\text{ ms} \pm 5\,\mu\text{s}$ ($1000\text{ Hz}$) |
| **Authority** | Untrusted (no direct actuator access) | **Trusted (sole motor gate authority)** |

: Processor dimension comparison. {#tbl-processor-comparison}

### Silicon-Level Privilege Isolation

On heterogeneous dual-brain silicon, the Linux application core and real-time core share fabric, so privilege must be enforced at the bus. Advanced motor timers and gate-driver enable pins are locked to the real-time domain via hardware peripheral firewalls, rendering them inaccessible to user-space Linux. The application processor talks to the microcontroller through a shared, non-cacheable SRAM ring buffer with mailbox interrupts and monotonic atomic sequence counters—lock-free, and without granting the MPU a path to the PWM registers.


## The Physical AI Co-Design Matrix

The conceptual foundation of this textbook is the **Physical AI Co-Design Matrix** (@fig-codesign-matrix): physical constraints on one axis, cognitive obligations on the other—not a serial handoff from mechanics to silicon to learning.

![The Physical AI Co-Design Matrix. Crossing physical reality with cognitive agency; every cell is a systems tension developed in later chapters.](figures/fig01_codesign_matrix.svg){#fig-codesign-matrix width=100%}

The columns, detailed in Chapter 2, are the physical walls that bound real-time machines: time and freshness, inertia and stopping, actuation and jerk, energy and thermal load, and silicon determinism on shared memory buses. The rows, formalized in Chapter 3, are the embodied cognitive lifecycle: perception, memory, reasoning, planning, and execution reflexes.

Read each cell as a *question*, not as a solved design. Perception meeting time asks when the observation happened and what the pixels cost to move (Chapter 4). Memory meeting inertia asks how uncertainty grows under occlusion. Reasoning meeting actuation asks how intent is bounded by reachability. Planning meeting silicon asks how action chunks amortize inference under bus contention. Execution meeting stopping asks how much braking margin remains, and how a bare-metal barrier filter projects untrusted proposals onto safe sets in under a millisecond (Chapters 2 and 8). This chapter only installs the compass.


## The Journey Ahead

The book follows an eleven-chapter progression across three parts (@fig-curriculum-blueprint). The evolutionary arc that places Physical AI after cloud ML, TinyML, and foundation-model deliberation is told in the preface; here we need only the chapter map.

![The Physical AI Curriculum and Chapter Blueprint. Foundations, embodied lifecycle, then placement, governance, and release.](figures/fig01_curriculum_blueprint.svg){#fig-curriculum-blueprint width=100%}

**Part I — Foundations (Chapters 1–3).** This chapter fixes the Causal Boundary. Chapter 2 develops time constants, freshness decay, and dynamic stopping kinematics, proving why tail latency governs survival. Chapter 3 formalizes the multi-rate runtime: slow semantic reasoning, mid-rate trajectory generation, and high-speed motor reflexes decoupled across shared-memory mailboxes.

**Part II — Embodied Lifecycle (Chapters 4–8).** We resolve the matrix row by row. Perception converts sensor streams into metric affordance tokens under DMA load. Memory maintains latent world models and frame trees under occlusion. Reasoning emits expiring intent leases from multimodal models. Planning bridges inference latency with diffusion policies, action chunks, and continuous jerk. Enforcement culminates in a real-time Control Barrier Function filter on bare-metal silicon.

**Part III — Placement, Governance, and Release (Chapters 9–11 and Capstone).** Placement maps the pipeline across heterogeneous silicon. Governance designs bumpless human authority and prevents policy collapse from untagged overrides. Assurance builds Claim-Argument-Evidence cases and seeded fault evidence for a deploy / condition / refuse verdict. The Capstone integrates the agent under live cross-layer faults.


## The Loop Charter

Before later chapters request motion, this chapter freezes what must already be true. The **loop charter** is the first record in the engineering notebook: it names the privilege split and the non-negotiable invariants the microcontroller will enforce.

| Subsystem | Trust Tier | Cadence | Physical Authority |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Proposal engine (MPU) | Untrusted | $1\text{ Hz}$ VLM $\to$ $20\text{ Hz}$ policy | Emits expiring proposals only; zero inverter authority |
| Permission authority (MCU) | Trusted | $1000\text{ Hz}$ enforcer | Sole PWM and gate-enable privilege; watchdog lease |

: Privilege split recorded in the loop charter. {#tbl-loop-privilege}

For the charter you must record platform values—not slogans—for a short must-record set:

1. Heartbeat / lease budget ($\tau_{\text{heartbeat}}$, $20\text{ ms}$ on the reference kit unless you measure otherwise).
2. Emergency deceleration path to Safe Torque Off when the heartbeat is lost.
3. Ban on dynamic heap allocation in the real-time loop.
4. Thermal or $I^2t$ current clamp.
5. Hard joint and velocity envelopes.
6. Rejection rule for stale or out-of-order proposals (freshness age).

Torque-rate and jerk clamps, full barrier certificates, and human-preemption wiring belong in the same notebook family, but they are detailed as templates rather than a second laundry list here. Templates live with the chapter materials; the bench lab asks you to freeze values for your platform.

::: {.callout-lab title="Closing the Causal Loop"}
On the Arduino UNO Q, prove that closing the physical loop introduces irreversible state mutation ($A_t \to W_{t+1} \to O_{t+1}$). Compare advisory mode, where proposals are rendered while motors stay cold, with actuating mode under microcontroller supervision. Advisory mode leaves the world unchanged; actuating mode displaces the mechanism and rewrites every later camera and encoder sample. Record the privilege split and the must-record invariant limits for your platform in the engineering notebook as the loop charter (`labs/01-close-the-loop`).
:::


## Systems Fallacies and Pitfalls

Four mistakes reverse the autopsy and the privilege split.

::: {.callout-warning}
### Common engineering fallacies in Physical AI

The digital sandbox fallacy treats a software exception as harmless because the operating system will catch it, yet timer peripherals can keep PWM latched after user space dies.

The monolithic end-to-end fallacy assumes that pixels-to-PWM eliminates classical control and real-time supervisors, yet stochastic models and operating-system tails still require an independent permission path.

The average throughput fallacy treats mean frames per second as a safety guarantee, yet a single $250\text{ ms}$ tail at $2.0\text{ m/s}$ is half a meter of blind motion.

The simulation-to-real equivalence fallacy treats high simulator success as a license for unconstrained bench deployment, yet inductance, backlash, bus contention, and irreversible heat are not optional.
:::


## Summary and What Comes Next

This chapter crossed the Causal Boundary into Physical AI. Digital undo is not physical irreversibility. Physical AI is learned authority over analog–digital command with irreversible consequence, and the same proposal–permission contract applies across an embodiment spectrum larger than robotics. Silicon and steel refuse the assumptions of simulation; untrusted proposals must be split from trusted permission; the co-design matrix and curriculum blueprint organize what follows. The loop charter freezes that privilege split as the first engineering-notebook record.

In Chapter 2 we put physical clocks on every microsecond of this pipeline, tracing photons from camera exposure through direct memory access, neural inference, and inter-process communication buffers to prove why mean latency is a dangerous metric and how information freshness ($\Delta t$) dictates dynamic stopping distance ($d_{\text{stop}}$).
